The literary production of the young members of Na Fianna Éireann, the warriors of Ireland, remains a century later an important case study in historical self-narration, in the construction of a common identity and in a counterculture opposed to the then-hegemonic British one. The Fianna were founded in 1909, at a moment when many European countries saw the birth of youth organisations devoted to moral, spiritual, physical and sometimes military training, with the common aim of overcoming the vices of modernity and preparing the coming generation for the imminent war; Baden-Powell's Boy Scouts are the most successful example. In opposition to these, fearing that Irish youth might be shaped by imperialist or Protestant organisations, Bulmer Hobson and Countess Constance Markievicz established a nationalist and Gaelic version of them. Members were mainly young Catholic males: the movement asserted its secularity, and Protestants and even Jews took part, but its nationalist stamp attracted Catholic youth above all; more complex was its relationship with girls, under-represented and at times excluded.
